title: Should you BOIL MILK before drinking? (Raw Milk vs Packet Milk)
description:
Milk is one of the most consumed foods on the planet—over six billion people drink it daily. But in India, milk is also surrounded by myths: should we boil milk that comes in packets? Does boiling destroy nutrients? What’s the difference between pasteurization, homogenization, and UHT treatment? And why are some people unable to digest milk at all?

In this episode, Pale Blue Thoughts unpacks the science of milk. From proteins like casein, calcium, and vitamins to processes like pasteurization (72°C for 15 seconds) and UHT treatment (138°C for 1–3 seconds), we explain how milk is made safe and how unnecessary boiling can reduce its nutritional value, particularly Vitamin B12. We also explore lactose intolerance, milk allergies, and why a genetic mutation thousands of years ago allowed some humans to keep digesting milk into adulthood.

If you’ve searched for “should we boil milk after pasteurization, milk myths India, UHT milk vs pasteurized milk, lactose intolerance explained, is milk healthy”, this video gives you the scientific perspective. Instead of wasting milk on rituals or depleting it of nutrients by over-boiling, we can use this nutrient-rich liquid to combat deficiencies and feed those who need it most.

Milk has shaped human evolution, agriculture, and nutrition. But separating facts from myths is crucial if we want to make better dietary choices. Don’t forget to like, share, comment, and subscribe for more everyday science myth-busting!

#MilkFacts #ScienceOfMilk #Pasteurization #LactoseIntolerance #PaleBlueThoughts

Chapters 
00:00 – Milk myths and misconceptions
02:00 – What milk is made of
04:00 – India: milk use & misuse
06:10 – Pasteurization, UHT & safety
08:30 – Should we boil milk at home?
10:20 – Lactose intolerance & allergies
12:20 – Milk products & plant alternatives

transcript: Hello and welcome to the 95th episode of Pale Blue Thoughts. Are you a milk lover? Please hear it carefully. I meant milk with a K as in Khalifa. Milk is nutrient-rich liquid food produced by the mammary glands of mammals. It is a primary source of nutrition for young mammals including breastfed human infants before they are able to digest solid food. Throughout the world, more than 6 billion people out of the total 7.9 billion consume milk and milk products. But how well do we know this liquid? As with anything else in India, there are a lot of misconceptions surrounding milk, too. Like, do we need to boil the milk before drinking? Why are some people unable to drink milk or eat milk products? Of course, there are plenty of YouTubers and the media out there who spread many myths without any scientific backing, which adds fuel to the misconceptions that we have carried forward from our forefathers. So, in this video, Pale Blue Thoughts discusses the scientific aspects of milk. Milk is an emulsion of fat globules within a water-based fluid that contains dissolved carbohydrates and protein along with minerals. Because it is produced as a food source for the young, all of its contents provide benefits for growth. The fat is mainly in the form of lipids. Normal bovine milk contains 30 to 35 g of protein per liter. The main protein found in milk is called casein, and that, when combined with the fat is what gives the milk its white color. Sheep and buffalo milk have a higher casein or protein content than cow milk or human milk, but they also contain more fat. A Babcock test is done to determine the fat content in milk, in which sulfuric acid is added to milk and then subjected to heating and centrifuging, which causes the fat to separate, which can then be measured. A normal cup of milk also contains around 20 to 30% of the calcium our body requires. Milk consumption occurs in two distinct ways. A natural source of nutrition for all babies of mammals, and a food product obtained from other mammals for consumption by humans of all ages. In almost all mammals, milk is fed to infants through breastfeeding. The early milk from mammals is called colostrum. Colostrum contains antibodies that provide protection to the newborn baby, as well as nutrients and growth factors. For humans, the World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and breastfeeding in addition to other food for up to 2 years of age or more. In many cultures, humans continue to consume milk beyond infancy using the milk of other mammals like cattle, goats, and sheep as a food product. But did you know that initially the ability to digest milk was limited to children as adults did not produce lactase, an enzyme necessary for digesting the lactose in milk. Lactase reaches its highest levels in the human small intestine after birth and then begins a slow decline unless milk is consumed regularly. People therefore converted milk to curd, cheese, and other products to reduce the levels of lactose. Thousands of years ago, a chance mutation spread in human populations in Europe that enabled the production of lactase in adulthood. This mutation allowed milk to be used as a new source of nutrition for adults, too. You can say we evolved to drink milk from being unable to do so a long time ago. Now, let us come to India specifically. India is the largest producer and consumer of cattle and buffalo milk in the world. However, when it comes to per capita consumption, India ranks much lower. One reason I strongly feel is this practice of wasting milk by pouring it over stone idols. Thousands of liters of nutrient-rich milk, which could have provided nutrition to millions of nutrient-deficient people in India, just goes down the drain. In rural India, milk is home delivered daily by local milkmen carrying bulk quantities in a metal container, usually on a bicycle. In other parts of metropolitan India, milk is usually delivered in plastic bags, glass bottles, or cartons via shops or supermarkets. Aside from cattle, many kinds of livestock provide milk used by humans for dairy products in India. These animals include buffalo, goat, sheep, camel, and donkey. Milk, when milk from a cow or buffalo contains many contaminants and bacteria, which are harmful to humans. These reach the animals through the fodder or the grass which the livestock grazes on. They also reach the cow's udder through feces which they eat while grazing and the water that they drink. These include bacteria like paratuberculosis, scarlet fever streptococci, typhoid bacilli, and E. coli. The way to get rid of it is through a process called pasteurization. This method was invented by French biologist and chemist Louis Pasteur, incidentally while experimenting to prevent wine and beer from souring, and the process was named after him. But before we understand pasteurization, there are two more processes which we need to understand with regards to milk processing. First is standardization, the mixing of milk from several different herds or dairies to produce a more consistent raw milk. Then there is homogenization, wherein the milk fat globules are reduced in size and dispersed uniformly through the rest of the milk. This is done by forcing the milk to push itself through small holes under high pressure, which breaks down the fat molecules and makes it more evenly spread in the milk. Pasteurization is a process by which milk is heated for a short time and then immediately cooling it. The standard high temperature short time process, also called as HTST, involves heating the milk to 70° C for 15 seconds, which completely kills the pathogenic bacteria in the milk, rendering it safe to drink for up to 3 weeks if continually refrigerated. A side effect of the heating of pasteurization is that some vitamin and mineral content is lost. Soluble calcium and phosphorus decrease by 5%, thiamine or vitamin B1 and vitamin B12 by 10%, and vitamin C by 20%. Because these losses are small in comparison to the large amount of the B1 and B12 present, milk continues to provide significant amount of thiamine and vitamin B12. The loss of vitamin C is not nutritionally significant as milk is not an important dietary source of vitamin C. Another method for treating milk is called UHT or ultra-high treatment. Ultra-high treatment is a type of milk processing where all bacteria are destroyed with high heat to extend its shelf life for up to 6 months as long as the package is not opened. Milk is firstly homogenized, which means it is treated to prevent the cream layer getting separated from the milk, and then it is heated to 138° C for 1 to 3 seconds. The milk is immediately cooled down and packed into a sterile container. As a result of this treatment, all the pathogenic bacteria within the milk are destroyed. The milk will now keep up for 6 months if unopened. UHT milk does not need to be refrigerated until the package is opened, which makes it easier to ship and store. But in this process, too, there is a loss of vitamin B1 and vitamin C, and there is also a slight change in the taste of the milk. Now, here is where Indian households boil the milk after opening the packet. Some do it out of habit, and some to make it last longer, and some say it removes the cream, and some say it enhances the taste. Whatever be the case, there is no need for you to boil the milk when it has been pasteurized or has undergone UHT. In fact, it may lead to a loss of nutrients as some studies suggest. A study conducted in 2011 and published in the Indian Journal of Public Health studied the effects of boiling milk using controls. It found that there was sufficient loss of nutrients each time the milk was boiled in Indian households. 15 minutes heating of milk has been reported to result in 24% losses of vitamin B12 in that study. If you are a vegetarian, then that loss is significant as you don't get the much-needed vitamin B12 from any other sources apart from meat. Diluting the milk with water was also found to reduce the nutritional profile. Links to several studies on the boiling of milk is given in the description as usual. So, if the milk that you receive is pasteurized or has undergone UHT and is stored and transported cleanly, there is no need for you to boil the milk again unless you want to drink it piping hot. But by doing so, you're depleting the milk of some of its nutrients. The The choice is yours. Looking at the prices of LPG these days, there is no cost-benefit advantage for you to boil the milk as soon as you open the milk packet. However, if you are in rural India and you receive milk directly from the farmer or goshala, please boil the milk before drinking. However, the story in India is a bit different. A 2011 survey by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India found that nearly 70% of samples had not conformed to the standards set for milk. The study found that due to lack of hygiene and sanitization in milk handling and packaging, detergents which were used during the cleaning operations were not washed properly and found their way into milk. About 8% of samples in the survey were found to have detergents which are hazardous to health. This is a different problem, which of course need to be addressed, but it is totally unrelated to the need of boiling milk. However, I have seen a lot of change in the dairy industry and today, many companies in India are ready to test the purity of milk in front of you. Lactose intolerance is a condition in which people have symptoms due to deficiency or absence of the enzyme lactase in the small intestine, causing poor absorption of lactose. People affected vary in the amount of lactose they can tolerate before symptoms develop, which may include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, gas, and nausea. Today, there are lactose-free versions available for those who suffer from this condition. The only noticeable difference of lactose-free milk from regular milk is a slightly sweeter taste. However, it does not contain more glucose and is nutritionally identical to regular milk. When raw milk is left standing for a while, it turns sour. This is a result of fermentation where lactic acid bacteria ferment the lactose in the milk into lactic acid, which makes the milk unpleasant to consume. But, humans have found ways to introduce specific bacteria to ferment the milk to produce a variety of fermented milk products such as cheese, yogurt, chaas or buttermilk, dahi, lassi, mattha, mishti doi, khoya, shrikhand, etc. Sometimes, milk is fortified by adding additional minerals and vitamins called as fortified milk. Today, we can also produce milk from plant sources such as coconut milk, almond milk, soy milk, etc., which is a boon for people with lactose intolerance or cow milk allergies. All said and done, it cannot be overlooked that milk has played a huge role in the evolution and development of mammals, including humans. They are the primary source of nutrients for all mammalian infants until they can eat other foods. In a country said to have around half of its population deficient in vitamin B12 as per studies due to its choice of food habit, it is important that as Indians, we do not further deplete the availability of vitamin B12 by boiling milk or wasting it down the drain. Hopefully, in the future, we will use this liquid to feed hungry children than pour it on top of stones or film cutouts, which is a pure waste of this nutrient-rich liquid. I hope you like this episode. If you did, please share this video so that others benefit from the information and also click on the subscribe button and the bell icon and select all to know when I release a new and informative video. Till we meet next time, it's bye-bye from Pale Blue Thoughts.
